query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the competition between the high mixing entropy and the interacting pairs that may drive chemical order, which can be controlled by adjusting the composition and introducing phase boundaries to achieve desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or annealed state
generation.intervention: Introduction of phase boundaries through composition adjustment or addition of alloying elements
generation.conditions: Varied temperatures (cryogenic to high-temperature) and environments (ambient to corrosive)
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries and precipitates (e.g., γ′ phase) that form due to composition adjustment
generation.mechanism: The high mixing entropy stabilizes the solid solution phase, while the interacting pairs drive chemical order, leading to the formation of phase boundaries and precipitates that enhance mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness due to the optimized phase stability and microstructure
generation.baseline: Single-phase high-entropy alloys without phase boundaries or precipitates
generation.boundary: The boundary of the hypothesis is limited to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys and may not be applicable to other alloy systems
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between composition, phase boundaries, and mechanical properties is still not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys with and without phase boundaries or precipitates, tested under varied temperatures and environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of phase boundaries or precipitates does not lead to improved mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

Unlike conventional alloys, which are typically based on one or two major elements, HEAs are stabilized by high mixing entropy, lowering the Gibbs free energy and favoring the formation of simple solid solution phases. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, HEAs also demonstrate superior thermal stability and corrosion resistance, making them highly suitable for use in harsh environments such as aerospace, nuclear power systems, and marine engineering [,]. Among the various HEA systems, FeCoNiCrMn has emerged as one of the most extensively studied, featuring a stable FCC structure []. Furthermore, refractory HEAs such as TiNbZrMoV and MoNbTaVW primarily form a single BCC solid solution and exhibit excellent high-temperature strength and phase stability [,].

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently emerged as new class of metallic materials with properties attractive for various structural and functional applications [,,,]. In particular, different HEAs demonstrate high strength and/or ductility at room and cryogenic temperatures, high specific strength at elevated temperatures, excellent fracture and impact toughness, wear resistance, etc. [,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Producing HEAs with a balanced combination of properties needed for practical applications still remains a significant challenge, however. Alloys based on the transition elements are the most studied type of HEAs []. One of the typical representatives of such HEAs is the equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy [,,]. Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
